planting.note: Sow seed (smoke-treated germination aids improve rates) on a sandy, nutrient-poor peat mix kept constantly wet with rain or distilled water in full sun and high heat; Byblis is a fast-growing warm-season annual best treated as a summer bog plant.

directions: Grow in a nutrient-poor, sandy peat mix kept permanently wet with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, in full sun and warm to hot conditions. Rainbow Plant gets its name from the way sunlight catches the sticky, glistening mucilage droplets covering its thin, wiry, upright leaves, creating tiny rainbow-colored reflections when viewed from the right angle, a passive flypaper-style trap unlike the active snapping or curling traps of many other carnivorous plants. Small five-petaled violet to pink flowers appear along the stems through the warm growing season. It is an Australian tropical annual that completes its life cycle in a single warm season, self-seeding readily in the growing tray if flowers are allowed to set seed; sow fresh seed the following spring once temperatures are reliably warm.

planting.note: Plant divisions in a well-drained, nutrient-poor mix of live sphagnum moss and perlite kept constantly moist with rain or distilled water; Heliamphora is a highland cloud-forest plant that wants cool nights, high humidity, and bright but indirect light rather than the hot full sun most other pitcher plants tolerate.

directions: Grow in a well-drained, nutrient-poor mix of live sphagnum moss and perlite kept constantly moist with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, in bright indirect light with high humidity and cool nights. Heliamphora nutans is native to the cool, misty tabletop mountains (tepuis) of Venezuela, forming simple, nodding, trumpet-shaped pitchers with a small spoon-shaped lid that does not close over the opening, catching rainwater and the insects that fall in and drown, rather than relying on digestive enzymes alone. Because of its cloud-forest origin, it struggles in the hot, dry conditions that suit lowland pitcher plants like Sarracenia and Nepenthes, doing best in a terrarium or greenhouse where temperature and humidity can be kept stable and moderate. Small white to pink bell-shaped flowers appear on tall stalks above the pitchers.

planting.note: Plant divisions in a wet, nutrient-poor mix of peat and sand kept constantly saturated with rain or distilled water; the corkscrew traps are entirely underground or submerged, so the growing medium must stay wet at all times.

directions: Grow in a wet, nutrient-poor mix of peat and sand kept constantly saturated with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, in full sun to bright light. Genlisea aurea is unique among commonly grown carnivorous plants for trapping its prey entirely underground: modified underground leaves form thin, spiraling, corkscrew-shaped tubes lined with tiny inward-pointing hairs that guide microscopic soil organisms in but prevent them from swimming back out, leading them toward a digestive bulb. Above ground the plant shows only a small rosette of ordinary leaves and, in season, bright yellow, snapdragon-like flowers on a thin stalk. Because its traps depend on constantly wet, saturated soil, the growing medium should never be allowed to dry even briefly, and standing water in a tray beneath the pot maintains the needed saturation.

planting.note: Plant divisions in a well-drained mineral mix of perlite, sand, and a small amount of peat; unlike bog-type carnivorous plants, this species wants the soil to dry slightly between thorough waterings, especially during its winter resting phase.

directions: Grow in a well-drained, mineral succulent-style mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, watering thoroughly but allowing the mix to dry slightly between waterings rather than keeping it constantly saturated like a bog plant. Esser's Butterwort is a miniature Mexican highland species forming a small, tight rosette of narrow, pale green, sticky-surfaced leaves that trap and digest tiny gnats, considerably smaller in scale than the larger, showier Pinguicula moranensis. Proportionally large, single purple-pink flowers rise on thin stalks well above the small rosette in spring. In winter it forms a smaller, tighter rosette of non-carnivorous succulent leaves and needs less water during this resting phase, resuming its sticky carnivorous leaves as growth resumes in spring; its Mexican highland origin gives it more tolerance of average tap water than typical bog carnivorous plants.
